title: Salt Sugar Fat: How the Food Giants Hooked Us
author: Michael Moss
target_audience: General readers interested in health, nutrition, and food
Individuals concerned about processed foods and diet
Students and professionals in public health, nutrition, and food studies
Consumers curious about the food industry’s influence on eating habits
core_themes: Manipulation of processed foods for craveability
The impact of salt, sugar, and fat on health
Corporate responsibility and profit-driven food engineering
Public health consequences of industrialized foods
primary_purpose: To expose how large food corporations engineer products with salt, sugar, and fat to maximize addiction and consumption, and to examine the public health crisis this creates.

structure_format.organization: Divided into thematic sections based on salt, sugar, and fat, with detailed case studies of companies and industry insiders
features: Firsthand interviews with industry executives and scientists

key_concepts_lessons: Processed food companies deliberately use salt, sugar, and fat to create products that are habit-forming and difficult to resist.
These ingredients not only enhance taste but also trigger biological responses that encourage overeating.
Corporate interests often prioritize profit over public health, resisting regulatory efforts and downplaying negative health effects.
Marketing, product engineering, and portion shaping are used to drive overconsumption.
Food industry strategies have contributed significantly to rising rates of obesity, diabetes, and related diseases.
Consumers are often unaware of how deeply manipulated processed foods are.
notable_features: Based on interviews and secret industry documents
Combines science, business, and consumer advocacy
Case studies of major brands and their products
Highlights the shift in public health policies
cultural_historical_context: Published during a growing awareness of the links between diet and public health crises in the United States and globally, and amidst increasing scrutiny of corporate influence on consumer habits and the obesity epidemic.
reception_impact: Critically acclaimed and a New York Times bestseller
Prompted debate on food regulation, labeling, and public health policy
Influenced other works and documentaries about processed food
Praised for its rigorous investigative reporting and readability
Critics acknowledge complexity of the food industry but note the book’s compelling exposé power
comparable_titles: Fast Food Nation by Eric Schlosser
The Omnivore’s Dilemma by Michael Pollan
The End of Overeating by David A. Kessler
